titleEn: Highway Multi-Vehicle Crash - Triage as the First-Arriving Crew

patient.name: Walter Brandt
patient.affectEn: P3, the focal patient: unrestrained pickup driver slumped forward against the steering wheel, unresponsive, snoring, blood and a broken denture in his mouth, pale and wet from the freezing rain
patient.speechEn: no words - he cannot answer; to a painful stimulus he makes only incomprehensible sounds. Every history answer comes from collateral sources (the 19-year-old witness, RCMP, the medical alert bracelet, the pill bottle and, later, his coworker)

scene.settingEn: Highway 1 eastbound near the 264th Street exit, Abbotsford, 0715 hrs, first light. Freezing rain, 0 degrees C, black ice. Three vehicles: a pickup against the median barrier with heavy front-end damage and fuel dripping from it; a sedan facing backwards in the slow lane with the driver's door caved in and the windshield starred; and an undamaged third car whose driver has stopped to help. Police have NOT yet closed the fast lane and vehicles are still passing at highway speed. FOUR patients. You are the FIRST ambulance; Abbotsford Fire and RCMP arrive with you; the second ambulance is 12 minutes out and a third 20 minutes out; Abbotsford Regional Hospital is 14 minutes away. EXAMINER NOTES: the candidate must count the patients, call for resources and triage all four before committing to one. The focal patient - the one this call is scored on - is P3. Transport category, packaging time, vital signs, history and treatment refer to P3 only: triage labels the candidate gives P1, P2 or P4, and any pulse or breathing check done on them during triage, are NOT P3's transport decision or vital signs.
hazardsEn: live traffic still passing at highway speed in the eastbound fast lane - do not enter the roadway until police block the lane or fire parks a blocking apparatus
cold exposure (0 degrees C, freezing rain) for patients and crew

bystanders.who: P1 - 19-year-old male, walking around (also the witness)
bystanders.knowsEn: On triage: walking and talking, small forehead laceration, keeps repeating "Is my girlfriend OK?" As a witness: the pickup crossed the centre line on the ice and hit the sedan head-on at highway speed, about 80 km/h, about four minutes before you arrived; the pickup driver was not wearing a seat belt and the pickup windshield is starred where his head hit; the driver has not moved or spoken since.

On triage: awake, seat-belt bruising across her chest, complains of chest pain, respirations 26, radial pulse weak and fast. She goes with the second ambulance; until then she needs someone (the fire first responders) with her, on oxygen.

bystanders.who: P4 - 7-year-old girl in a booster seat in the sedan
bystanders.knowsEn: On triage: crying loudly, no visible injury. She needs an adult with her (fire first responders) until the third ambulance arrives.

bystanders.who: driver of the undamaged third car
bystanders.knowsEn: Stopped to help; uninjured; saw nothing more than the witness. Will help if given a simple, safe task off the roadway.
Arrive with you. Can park an engine as a blocker, extricate P3 onto a scoop or long board with you, and monitor P2, P4 and P1 under your direction until the next ambulances arrive.

Arrive with you; will close the fast lane and control traffic when asked. They hand you a medical alert bracelet from the pickup driver reading 'Atrial fibrillation - warfarin', a pill bottle from the door pocket labelled warfarin 5 mg and metoprolol 50 mg, and his wallet, which gives his date of birth - he is 62. They have no allergy information.

bystanders.who: P3's coworker (follows in a truck and arrives during the call)
bystanders.knowsEn: Collateral only if asked: he has been well and works full time; no known seizures or strokes; on warfarin for an irregular heart; smoker who gets short of breath on stairs; atrial fibrillation on metoprolol; nothing known about bowels or bladder or skin; old back injury; not diabetic; wears glasses (found on the dash). Does not know any allergies or when he last ate.

scene.partnerEn: one partner at your licence level; acts only on your delegation
equipmentEn: PCP: IV start kit, normal saline and TXA

dispatchEn: 0715 hrs. Code 3 to Highway 1 eastbound near the 264th Street exit, Abbotsford. Three vehicles, freezing rain and black ice, multiple patients reported. You are the FIRST ambulance on scene. Abbotsford Fire and RCMP are arriving at the same time as you. The second ambulance is 12 minutes out and a third is 20 minutes out. Abbotsford Regional Hospital is 14 minutes away.
dispatchUpdateEn: En-route update: callers report a pickup truck crossed the centre line on ice and struck a sedan; one person is 'not waking up' and a child is in one of the cars. Traffic is still moving in the eastbound fast lane.
arrivalEn: You are the first ambulance. Abbotsford Fire and RCMP pull up at the same time. Freezing rain, 0 degrees C, first light, black ice on the road. Three vehicles: a pickup against the median barrier with heavy front-end damage and fuel dripping from it; a sedan facing backwards in the slow lane with the driver's door caved in and the windshield starred; an undamaged third car whose driver has stopped to help. Police have not closed the fast lane yet - vehicles are still passing at highway speed.
firstLookEn: From the protected side: a young man is walking around between the vehicles holding his forehead; a woman is awake in the sedan's driver's seat; a child is crying loudly in a booster seat in the back of the sedan; and in the pickup a man is slumped forward over the steering wheel, motionless, with loud snoring coming from the cab. Glass and fuel on the wet road; traffic still passing in the fast lane.

primary.locEn: P3: no response to your voice. To a painful stimulus he makes only incomprehensible sounds and withdraws; his eyes stay closed (GCS E1 V2 M4). He cannot protect his own airway. The scenario calls him unresponsive - accept 'U' (or 'P' with the pain response described).
primary.airwayEn: Snoring respirations - the tongue is obstructing. Blood and a broken denture in the mouth. A jaw thrust WITHOUT head tilt opens the airway and the snoring stops; suction clears the blood; the broken denture has to come out; an OPA is tolerated - there is no gag reflex. If the airway is not opened and cleared, the snoring continues and turns to gurgling.
primary.breathingEn: Respirations 8 and shallow - INADEQUATE; chest rise minimal. SpO2 84% on room air. If the candidate assists with a BVM at 10-12 per minute with 15 L and the reservoir: good chest rise with each breath and SpO2 96%. A non-rebreather alone does not fix this - the rate stays 8 and shallow.
primary.circulationEn: Carotid pulse 124, weak; radial pulse present but thready. Steady bleeding from a scalp laceration (see the RBS). Skin pale, cool, clammy - shock.
primary.rbsEn: Head: 8 cm forehead/scalp laceration bleeding steadily - controlled with direct pressure and a dressing; boggy swelling over the right temple. Pupils if checked now: right 5 mm and sluggish, left 3 mm and reactive. Chest: bruising over the sternum from the steering wheel. Abdomen: bruising across the upper abdomen from the wheel; soft. Right forearm deformed and swollen, radial pulse present. Both knees struck the dash; the right knee is swollen. No other external hemorrhage. Unconscious, unrestrained driver with a starred windshield: spinal precautions ARE indicated. Skin is given automatically during the RBS: pale, cool, clammy.

fe.cnsEn: Coworker (collateral): "No seizures or strokes that I know of. He's on warfarin for an irregular heart."

findings.headNeckEn: 8 cm scalp laceration to the forehead, now dressed and no longer bleeding through; boggy swelling over the right temple; blood and the broken denture already cleared from the mouth; no CSF from the ears or nose. Neck: trachea midline, no JVD; collar applied and rechecked.
findings.chestLungsEn: No seat-belt marks (unrestrained); bruising over the sternum from the steering wheel; air entry equal but decreased at both bases (with BVM ventilation).
findings.abdomenEn: Soft; bruising across the upper abdomen from the steering wheel.
findings.backEn: Checked during the log roll onto the scoop: no step, no deformity.
findings.lowerExtremitiesEn: Both knees struck the dash; the right knee is swollen. Pedal pulses present in both feet.
findings.upperExtremitiesEn: Deformed and swollen right forearm with a radial pulse present. Left arm unremarkable.

vitalsSets.pupils: right 5 mm and sluggish, left 3 mm and reactive

vitalsSets.unlockNoteEn: en route, ventilated and warmed (0734 in the model timeline); GCS slightly better, pupils unchanged

stateChanges.examinerLineEn: Fire has parked the engine across the fast lane as a blocker and RCMP are closing the lane. You can now work from the protected side.
The pickup driver's snoring has turned to gurgling through the blood in his mouth, and his lips look dusky.
His own breathing is still only about 8 a minute and shallow - the chest barely moves - and he is getting duskier.
Nobody is holding his head now - it rolls to the side as he is moved.
The second ambulance pulls up behind the fire engine. Its crew asks you: "What have you got, and who do you want us to take?"

expected.actionEn: Acknowledge and state your plan out loud: as the first crew you triage everyone before treating anyone, then commit to the highest-priority patient
Ask dispatch for the number of patients, request additional ambulances early, and confirm fire is assigned for extrication and police for traffic control
Anticipate live traffic, black ice, fuel and glass; PPE including high-visibility outerwear before stepping out of the ambulance
Verbalize hazards (live traffic, black ice, leaking fuel, glass), environment (freezing rain), MOI (high-speed head-on on ice) and the number of patients - FOUR
Do not enter the roadway until police block the lane or fire parks a blocking apparatus; work from the protected side
Global visual sweep before touching anyone: who is walking, who is talking, who is silent
Triage all four: P3 unresponsive with a compromised airway is FIRST, P2 with chest trauma and shock signs is second, P4 the crying child is third, P1 the walking wounded is last
Report the patient count and severity to dispatch and confirm the additional ambulances; assign the fire first responders to monitor P2 and stay with P4 and P1 until relieved
Assess LOC / AVPU: Unresponsive
Take manual C-spine control from behind BEFORE moving the head or opening the airway - unconscious trauma patient in a high-speed MVC
Open and clear the airway: jaw thrust without head tilt, suction the blood, remove the broken denture, insert an OPA
Recognize inadequate respirations at 8 shallow and assist ventilation immediately with a BVM at 10-12/min with 15 L and reservoir
Assess circulation: carotid and radial pulses, recognize shock
Rapid body survey head to toe and control the scalp hemorrhage with direct pressure and a dressing
Note skin: pale, cool, clammy
triggers: skin is pale cool and clammy

expected.actionEn: Oxygen 15 L through the BVM reservoir - a non-rebreather is not enough for a patient who is not breathing adequately
Rapid extrication with fire assistance onto a scoop or long board, kept in line, then supine with the airway managed and blankets on
Categorize P3 as RTC and transport him first
Packaged and ready to be lifted onto the cot within 15 minutes despite the extrication
Hand over scene command and the triage assignments to the incoming crews and dispatch before you leave
triggers: second crew takes the sedan driver

expected.actionEn: State the chief complaint as an unresponsive trauma patient with head injury after a high-speed head-on collision
HxC/C from witnesses and police: speed, restraint use, windshield starring, compartment intrusion, whether he has been moved, and how long he has been unresponsive
triggers: was he wearing a seat belt
how long has he been unresponsive

expected.actionEn: PMHx from the medical alert bracelet: atrial fibrillation - and recognize that anticoagulation makes this head injury far more dangerous
Medications from the pill bottle: warfarin 5 mg and metoprolol 50 mg (a beta blocker can blunt the tachycardic response to blood loss); take the bottle to hospital
Allergies: unobtainable - document as unknown rather than skipping the question
Last oral intake: unknown, warm coffee in the vehicle - document what you observed
Pain scale cannot be obtained; document why and use objective findings instead
GCS with all three components scored separately - this is the number the trauma team will compare against
Blood pressure by auscultation
Pulse rate, strength and rhythm
Respirations - rate, depth and adequacy, documented before and after assistance
Skin assessed hands-on
Pupils - the unequal sluggish right pupil is a critical finding to report
SpO2 recorded with the device and flow rate
Blood glucose - indicated in any patient with an altered level of consciousness
Temperature - indicated after prolonged exposure to freezing rain
FE - General health (collateral)
FE - CNS (collateral)
FE - Respiratory (collateral)
FE - Cardiovascular (collateral: atrial fibrillation on warfarin)
FE - GI/GU (document as unobtainable)
FE - Integumentary (objective findings only)
FE - Musculoskeletal (collateral)
FE - Endocrine (not diabetic - supports the normal BGL)
FE - EENT (collateral)
Head and neck: scalp wound, temporal swelling, ears and nose for CSF, trachea and collar check
Chest with auscultation at six sites
Abdomen - steering wheel bruising in an unrestrained driver
Back inspected and palpated during the log roll
Upper extremities including distal pulse in the deformed forearm
triggers: radial pulse in the right arm

expected.actionEn: Lower extremities including pedal pulses
Airway management skill: suction, OPA, jaw thrust maintained, airway rechecked after every move
Breathing management skill: BVM at 10-12 per minute with 15 L and reservoir, watching chest rise, avoiding hyperventilation and gastric insufflation
Spinal management skill: manual control, collar, scoop or board, head blocks and straps, manual control released only when fully secured
Wound management skill: dressing and pressure on the scalp laceration, monitored for re-bleeding in an anticoagulated patient
Fracture management skill: splint the right forearm with distal pulse checks before and after, without delaying transport
Head injury management: ventilate at a normal rate, keep SpO2 up, avoid hypotension, and transport without delay
Verbalize that Entonox and methoxyflurane are contraindicated with a decreased LOC and head injury, and that nothing goes by mouth
Reassess ABCs and the airway adjunct after the extrication and after every move
triggers: recheck the airway after the move

expected.actionEn: Second complete set of vitals within 5-6 minutes, with GCS and pupils compared against the first set
Recheck the scalp dressing and the splinted forearm's distal circulation
triggers: distal circulation in the right hand

expected.actionEn: Keep ventilating at a normal rate and keep him warm - do not hyperventilate and do not let him get cold
En-route notification: unconscious head injury with unequal pupils on warfarin, plus a heads-up that three more patients are coming
Complete hand-off including mechanism, restraint status, GCS trend, pupils, airway interventions and anticoagulation
Accurate PCR within 5 minutes documenting both the triage assignments and this patient's care

specialEvents.descriptionEn: candidate actually opens and clears P3's airway: jaw thrust, suction, removing the broken denture, or inserting an OPA/NPA
candidate (or the partner on direction) actually starts assisting P3's breathing with a BVM / positive-pressure ventilations
candidate asks police to close the fast lane / control traffic, or asks fire to park a blocking apparatus, before working near the roadway
candidate starts treating any patient (for example dressing P1's forehead or putting oxygen on P2) before counting all four patients and requesting additional resources
after triage the candidate commits to P1, P2 or P4 instead of P3, or leaves P3 with an unmanaged airway to treat someone else
candidate (or the partner on direction) walks into the open eastbound fast lane before police have closed it or fire has parked a blocking apparatus
candidate states that spinal precautions are not needed for P3, or moves, extricates or log-rolls P3 with nobody holding manual c-spine control at any point
candidate moves P3's head, opens his airway, or applies a painful stimulus before anyone is holding manual c-spine control
candidate uses a head-tilt chin-lift on P3 instead of a jaw thrust without head tilt
candidate (or the partner on the candidate's instruction) lets go of manual c-spine control before P3 is fully secured with collar, head blocks and straps on the scoop or board
candidate ventilates P3 clearly faster than about 12 per minute (for example squeezing continuously, every 2-3 seconds, or 20 or more per minute)
candidate keeps P3 on scene to splint the forearm or perfect the packaging instead of splinting during packaging or en route
candidate leaves with P3 without assigning anyone (fire first responders) to monitor P2, P4 and P1, or without reporting them to dispatch and the incoming crews
candidate gives P3 anything by mouth (oral glucose, tablets, fluids)
PCP runs the saline bolus past 500 mL or onto the next bag without reassessing the patient (BP / vitals / ABCs) in between

drugs.doseEn: self-administered inhalation - CONTRAINDICATED here: altered level of consciousness (record only if actually given)
3 mL self-administered via inhaler per guideline - CONTRAINDICATED here: decreased level of consciousness and head injury (record only if actually given)
300-400 mg PO per guideline - CONTRAINDICATED here: he takes an anticoagulant (warfarin), and nothing goes by mouth in an unresponsive patient (record only if actually given)
500-1000 mg PO per guideline - not for this unresponsive patient: nothing by mouth (record only if actually given)

PCP: 2 g (2000 mg) IV push over 1 minute if indicated within the 3-hour window (injury at 0711); contraindicated for an isolated TBI - this patient also has shock with steering-wheel bruising to the chest and abdomen
drugs.contraindicationsEn: known hypersensitivity or allergy to TXA; more than 3 hours after injury; patient under 12 years; isolated TBI

drugs.doseEn: PCP: vascular access en route; 20 mL/kg bolus to a maximum of 2 L, reassessing every 500 mL, while he stays hypotensive - hypotension is devastating in a head injury

examinerPrompts.locNotDepictedEn: He does not respond to your voice. To a painful stimulus he groans incomprehensibly and pulls away; his eyes stay closed.
examinerPrompts.breathingNotDepictedEn: He is breathing only about 8 times a minute, shallow, with loud snoring and gurgling from the blood in his mouth; the chest barely moves.
examinerPrompts.missedInjuryEn: You have his airway and breathing managed - what did your rapid body survey find from head to toe?

trackNotes.emrEn: In BC an EMR crew is often the first ambulance on a highway crash: count the patients, call for what you need before you are buried in patient care, triage by ABCs, assign the fire first responders to the others, then deliver excellent basic care to the sickest one. Everything P3 needs is EMR scope - manual c-spine, suction, OPA, jaw thrust, BVM ventilation, collar and scoop/board, hemorrhage control, splinting, warmth and a 15-minute package. An IV with fluids and TXA are PCP-only and are not EMR answers. Entonox and methoxyflurane are contraindicated (decreased LOC, head injury); nothing by mouth.
trackNotes.pcpEn: PCP adds vascular access en route, a 20 mL/kg normal saline bolus to a maximum of 2 L reassessed every 500 mL while he stays hypotensive (hypotension is devastating in a head injury), TXA 2 g IV over 1 minute only if indicated within the 3-hour window (TXA is contraindicated for an isolated TBI), and the Functional Enquiry from collateral sources. Airway, ventilation rate and spinal care are identical.

sourcePages: Scenario etr-09 (data/practical/emr-trauma-2.json): dispatch, scene (four patients, triage findings), primary, transport, history (collateral), vitals sets 1-2, FE (collateral), exam, interventions, ongoing, handoff, critical pitfalls, EMR/PCP variants. BC Provincial Examination Guidelines (current to June 15, 2026): p.7 Findings in Unstable Adult Patients (altered LOC or unconsciousness, difficulty maintaining the airway, cool pale clammy skin secondary to shock, new onset neurological deficits); p.11 Primary Survey intervention indications (c-spine stabilization for an unconscious patient where trauma cannot be ruled out; airway maintenance and suctioning; assisting shallow or slow respirations); p.13 AVPU (unresponsive patient cannot protect own airway); p.25 Spinal Management (manual stabilization, hard collar, spinal immobilization device, foam blocks, secure the body); p.27 Traumatic Brain Injuries (GCS 8 or less = severe; SpO2 94% or above; assist ventilations; PCP: maintain systolic over 120; TXA contraindicated for isolated TBI); p.42 (avoid hyperventilation); p.54 Hypovolemia (PCP 20 mL/kg to a maximum of 2 L reassessing every 500 mL); p.65 Entonox (contraindication: altered LOC); p.68 Ibuprofen (contraindication: anticoagulants); p.71 Methoxyflurane (contraindication: decreased LOC or head injury); p.78 Tranexamic Acid (2 g IV over 1 minute; contraindicated for isolated TBI and more than 3 hours after injury). EMALB Practical Examination Grading Criteria timing rules (priority patient ready to be lifted onto the cot in 15 minutes).
